en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Mahāvagga 2.
Uposathakkhandhaka (The Chapter on the Observance)
1. The Permission for Assemblies.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, wanderers of other sects used to assemble on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight and discourse on the Dhamma.
Those people approach to hear the Dhamma.
They gain affection for the wanderers of other sects, they gain confidence in them, and those wanderers of other sects gain a following.
Then, while King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“Now, wanderers of other sects gather on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight and speak Dhamma.
People approach them to listen to the Dhamma.
They gain affection for those wanderers of other sects, they gain confidence in them, and those wanderers of other sects gain a following.”
"Perhaps, venerable sir, the noble ladies might also assemble on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind: ‘At present,
wanderers of other sects gather on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight and speak on the Dhamma.’”
People approach them to hear the Dhamma.
They gain affection for the wanderers of other sects, they gain confidence in them, and those wanderers of other sects gain a following.
What if the masters were also to assemble on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight?”
“It would be well, venerable sir, if the noble ones were also to assemble on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight.
Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this connection, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to assemble on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight.
Now at that time, the bhikkhus—
“Since it has been permitted by the Blessed One that we may assemble on the fourteenth, the fifteenth,
and the eighth day of the fortnight,” they would assemble on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight and sit in silence.
Then those people would approach them to hear the Dhamma.
They complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
"How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyan, having assembled on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight, sit in silence like dumb pigs?
Should not the Dhamma indeed be spoken by those who have assembled?"
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and expressing their indignation.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ...Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, to assemble on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight to recite the Dhamma.
2. The Allowance for the Recitation of the Pātimokkha Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“What if I were to authorize for them the recitation of the Pātimokkha consisting of those training rules that have been laid down by me for the bhikkhus?
That will serve as their Uposatha ceremony.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and, having given a Dhamma talk on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Here, monks, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘What if I were to authorize the recitation of the Pātimokkha for those training rules that I have laid down for the monks?
That will serve as their Uposatha ceremony.’”
"I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha.
And thus, monks, it should be recited:
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha."
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.
What is the preliminary duty for the Saṅgha?”
Venerable sirs, announce your purity.
I shall recite the Pātimokkha.
Let all of us who are present listen well and pay close attention.
Whoever has committed an offense should disclose it.
One who has no offense should remain silent.
By your silence, I shall know that you venerable ones are pure.
Just as there is an answer when one is questioned individually, even so, in such an assembly, the proclamation is made up to three times.
Now, whichever monk, while the proclamation is being made for the third time, remembers an existing offense and does not disclose it, that is a deliberate lie.
And, venerable friends, a deliberate lie has been called by the Blessed One an obstructive state.
"Therefore, a monk who remembers [an offense], who has committed one, and who desires purification, should disclose that offense while it still exists;
for when it has been disclosed, he finds ease. Thus [ends the section on] the Pātimokkha.
This is the beginning, this is the source, this is the foremost of wholesome states. Therefore it is called the *pātimokkha*.
"Venerable ones" (*āyasmanto*) is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a designation for those who possess reverence and deference; thus it is said, "venerable ones."
"I shall point out" means I shall announce, teach, prescribe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and make manifest. "That" refers to...
The *pātimokkha* is what is spoken.
"All those who are present" means as many as there are elders, novices, and those of middle standing in that assembly; these are called "all those who are present."
"Let us listen attentively":
having made it our bone, having made it our mind, we attend with our whole heart.
"We attend": [we apply our minds].
With one-pointed minds, with undistracted minds, and with unperturbed minds, let us listen.

Whoever may have committed an offense—whether it be an elder, a novice, or one of middle standing; whether it be an offense belonging to any of the five classes of offenses, or an offense belonging to any of the seven classes of offenses.
"Should reveal" means:
he should teach it, he should uncover it, he should make it plain, he should explain it—either in the midst of the Saṅgha, or in the midst of a group, or to an individual.
"Non-existent offense" means: [an offense that does not exist].
Either she has not committed an offense, or having committed one, she has emerged from it.
"One should remain silent" means that one should consent by remaining silent and should not speak.

"I shall know" means "I shall understand"; "I shall bear [it in mind]" means "I shall maintain it. And as for the manner in which there is an explanation when one is questioned individually: [the Blessed One said: "In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu who has heard much, who has retained what he has heard, who has stored up what he has heard; who has learned much, who possesses the Dhamma, who is a knower of the Dhamma, who dwells supported by the Dhamma, who relies on the Dhamma, not on another, nor on another teacher... [and so forth]. This is the explanation when one is questioned individually. Thus, Ānanda, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in brief. Having heard that Dhamma from the Blessed One, the Venerable Ānanda reflected upon it. As he was reflecting, the Venerable Ānanda attained the four jhānas—states of pure mindfulness and happiness in the present life—which are supramundane and ripen in the higher realms. Then, having emerged from the fourth jhāna, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Venerable Upavāṇa: "Friend Upavāṇa, the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma in brief... [as above]... Thus, friend, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in brief. Having heard that Dhamma from the Blessed One, I reflected upon it. As I was reflecting, I attained the four jhānas—states of pure mindfulness and happiness in the present life—which are supramundane and ripen in the higher realms. Come, friend Upavāṇa, let us go to the Blessed One and report this matter to him. "As you say, friend," the Venerable Upavāṇa replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the two venerable ones went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, they sat down at one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Upavāṇa reported this matter to the Blessed One. "It is wonderful, Upavāṇa! It is marvelous, Upavāṇa! How well this was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda! For indeed, Upavāṇa, if a bhikkhu has heard much, has retained what he has heard, has stored up what he has heard; if he has learned much, possesses the Dhamma, is a knower of the Dhamma, dwells supported by the Dhamma, relies on the Dhamma, not on another, nor on another teacher; if he is virtuous, possessed of noble virtue; if he is learned, possessing what has been heard; if he is a forest-dweller, one who frequents remote lodgings; if he is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and requisites for the sick; if he is energetic in abandoning unwholesome states and striving toward wholesome states, possessed of unflagging energy, firm in endeavor, not casting off the burden of wholesome qualities; if he is established in mindfulness, possessing supreme mindfulness and circumspection, one who remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago; if he is wise, possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering: then, Upavāṇa, such a bhikkhu would be capable of declaring final knowledge even before the Tathāgata. "It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well this was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda!

For indeed, Blessed One, if a bhikkhu has heard much... [as above]... then, Blessed One, such a bhikkhu would be capable of declaring final knowledge even before the Tathāgata. "Upavāṇa, if a bhikkhu has heard much... [as above]... then, Upavāṇa, such a bhikkhu would be capable of declaring final knowledge even before the Tathāgata. [The Blessed One said: "In this case, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu who has heard much... [as above]... then, Upavāṇa, such a bhikkhu would be capable of declaring final knowledge even before the Tathāgata. "Blessed One, I am not capable of declaring final knowledge even before the Blessed One. "Upavāṇa, how could you not be capable? For, Upavāṇa, if a bhikkhu has heard much... [as above]... then, Upavāṇa, such a bhikkhu would be capable of declaring final knowledge even before the Tathāgata. [as above]... then, Upavāṇa, such a bhikkhu would be capable of declaring final knowledge even before the Tathāgata. [as above]... then, Upavāṇa, such a bhikkhu would be capable of declaring final knowledge even before the Tathāgata. [as above]... then, Upavāṇa, such
Just as one person, when questioned by another, would answer, even so it should be understood by that assembly: "He is questioning me.
An assembly of such a kind is called a "bhikkhu assembly."
"Up to the third proclamation has been made" means:
it has been proclaimed once, it has been proclaimed a second time, and it has been proclaimed a third time.
"One who remembers" means...
Knowing and clearly perceiving:
there is indeed an offense that has been committed, or having committed it, one has not emerged from it.
"Should not explain" means he should not teach, should not disclose, should not make clear, should not reveal it either in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or to an individual.
"There is an intentional falsehood for him" means...
What is the offense for intentional lying? It is a *dukkaṭa*.
"It has been stated by the Blessed One that this is an obstructive factor."
What is obstructive?
It is obstructive to the attainment of the first jhāna; it is obstructive to the attainment of the second jhāna;
it is obstructive to the attainment of the third jhāna; it is obstructive to the attainment of the fourth jhāna.

It is an obstacle to the attainment of the meditative absorptions (jhānas), the liberations (vimokkhas), the concentrations (samādhis), the attainments (samāpattis), renunciations (nekkhammas), the ways of escape (nissaraṇas),
the seclusions (pavivekas), and wholesome states (dhammas). Therefore...
"Because of that.
"By one who remembers" means by one who knows and by one who recognizes.
"By one desiring purification" means by one who wishes to emerge [from the offense] and wishes to become pure. An "offense" (āpatti) is so called because it falls upon [the person].
"Has fallen into [an offense]" means she has committed one; "or having fallen into it, has not emerged from it.
"Should be disclosed" means it should be disclosed either in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or before a single person.
For it is easy for him when he has disclosed [his faults]. Easy for what?
It is easy for the attainment of the first jhāna; it is easy for the attainment of the second jhāna.
It is conducive to the attainment of the third jhāna; it is conducive to the attainment of the fourth jhāna;
it is conducive to the attainment of the jhānas, the liberations, the concentrations, the attainments, the renunciations, the departures, the seclusions, and all wholesome states.
Now at that time, thinking,
"The Blessed One has authorized the recitation of the Pātimokkha," the monks recited the Pātimokkha every day.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited every day.
Whoever should recite it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
“I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha on the Uposatha day.
Now at that time, the monks, thinking,
“The Blessed One has allowed the recitation of the Pātimokkha on the Uposatha day,” [proceeded accordingly].
They recited the Pātimokkha three times a fortnight—on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited three times a fortnight.”
"Whoever should recite it [more than once], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha once every half-month, either on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks recited the Pātimokkha according to their respective assemblies, each in his own assembly.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited according to the assembly; it should be recited by each respective assembly.
Whoever should recite it otherwise incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
“I allow you, monks, a Uposatha ceremony for those who are in concord.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“It has been prescribed by the Blessed One—”
‘The Uposatha ceremony for those who are in concord.
To what extent, then, is there concord—is it as far as a single residence, or indeed the whole earth?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, that there is concord as long as there is a single residence.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākappina was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi Deer Park.
Then, while the Venerable Mahākappina was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Should I go to the Uposatha or not? Should I go to the Sangha transaction or not? For I am indeed pure with the highest purity.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the Venerable Mahākappina’s mind—
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so,
vanishing from Vulture Peak Mountain, he reappeared before the Venerable Mahākappina in the Maddakucchi Deer Park.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The Venerable Mahākappina, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Mahākappina was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Kappina, did it not occur to you while you were alone in seclusion this reflection in your mind:
‘I might go to the Uposatha or I might not go; I might go to the Sangha transaction or I might not go; yet I am pure with the highest purity’?
“It was so, Bhante.”
“If you brahmins do not honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Uposatha, then who indeed will honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Uposatha?
Go away, brahmin, to your Uposatha; do not come to ours.
Go away, brahmin, to your Saṅgha business; do not come to ours.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Mahākappina replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One— instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Mahākappina with a discourse on the Dhamma—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm— disappeared from that place.
In this very way—having vanished from the presence of the Venerable Mahākappina at the Maddakucchi Deer Park, he reappeared on Vulture Peak Mountain.
4. The Authorization of the Boundaries.
Then, this thought occurred to the bhikkhus:
“The Blessed One has prescribed:
‘To this extent there is concord: as long as there is a single residence. To what extent, then, does there exist a single residence?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to designate a boundary.
And how, monks, should it be designated?
First, the landmarks must be proclaimed:”
The mountain sign, the rock sign, the forest sign, the tree sign, the path sign, the anthill sign, the river sign, and the water sign.
Having announced these signs, a learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
To whatever extent the boundary marks have been described all around:
if it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha, by means of these boundary marks, establish a zone for common residence and a single Uposatha.
This is the motion.
"Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs.
To whatever extent the markers have been proclaimed all around,
the Sangha designates the boundary by these markers as a common residence with a single Uposatha."
Whichever venerable one approves of the designation of this boundary as a common residence with a single Uposatha by means of these marks, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The boundary has been designated by the Saṅgha by means of these marks as a common residence with a single Uposatha.
“It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, thinking, “The Blessed One has authorized the formal act of establishing a boundary,” [proceeded to do so].
They were designating extremely large boundaries—some four yojanas, some five yojanas, and some six yojanas.
Monks coming for the Uposatha would arrive while the Pātimokkha was being recited, or they would arrive as soon as it had been recited, or they would stay overnight along the way.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a boundary should not be authorized that is too large—neither four yojanas, nor five yojanas, nor six yojanas.
Whoever should authorize one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to authorize a boundary of a maximum of three yojanas.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were delimiting a boundary on the far side of a river.
As the monks were coming for the uposatha, they were being swept away, their alms-bowls were being swept away, and their robes were being swept away.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a river-bank boundary should not be authorized.
Whoever should authorize one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, I allow you to authorize such a river-bank boundary where there is either a permanent boat-landing or a permanent bridge.”
5. Discussion on the Uposatha Hall Now at that time, the monks were reciting the Pātimokkha in the vicinity of the monasteries without having made an appointment.
The visiting monks did not know [where it was being recited].
“Where will the Uposatha be performed today?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, the Pātimokkha must not be recited in the vicinity of a monastery without a prior agreement.”
Whoever should designate [one] commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Monks, I allow you to perform the Uposatha after having formally authorized a Uposatha hall—whether it be a monastery (*vihāra*), a gabled house (*aḍḍhayoga*), a multi-storied building (*pāsāda*), a watchtower (*hammiya*), or a cave (*guha*)—whichever the Saṅgha desires.
And furthermore, monks, it should be authorized in this way.
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should authorize such-and-such a dwelling as the Uposatha hall.”
This is the motion.
Let the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me.
The Sangha authorizes the dwelling named so-and-so as the Uposatha hall.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of this dwelling as an Uposatha hall, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
This dwelling, [named] so-and-so, has been appointed by the Saṅgha as an Uposatha hall.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
Now at that time, in a certain residence, two Uposatha halls had been authorized.
The monks assembled in both places.
“‘The Uposatha will be performed here; the Uposatha will be performed there.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
‘Monks, two Uposatha halls should not be authorized in a single residence.’”
Whoever should appoint one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, having dismissed one [monk], to perform the Uposatha at one place.
And thus, monks, should he be dismissed:
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha may abolish this Uposatha hall named so-and-so."
This is the motion.
Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs:
the Sangha abolishes the Uposatha hall named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable one approves of the abolition of this Uposatha hall named so-and-so, let him be silent;
whichever does not approve, let him speak.
The Sangha has abolished the Uposatha hall named so-and-so.
“It is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this. 6.

The Authorization for a Large Uposatha Hall Now at that time, in a certain monastery, a very small Uposatha hall had been authorized. On the day of the Uposatha, a large community of monks had assembled there.
The bhikkhus, sitting on ground that had not been formally authorized, heard the Pātimokkha.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"It has been laid down by the Blessed One—"
“Having designated a Uposatha hall, the Uposatha should be performed. Yet we sat on ground that had not been designated and recited the Pātimokkha; was our Uposatha performed, or was it not?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, whether they are sitting on ground that has been designated or on ground that has not been designated, as long as they hear the Pātimokkha, their Uposatha is performed.”
"Therefore, monks, let the Saṅgha appoint as large a boundary for the Uposatha as it desires.
And thus, monks, should it be appointed:
first, the landmarks must be proclaimed."
Having announced the boundary markers, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
As far as the boundary markers have been announced all around.”
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize these signs as the face of the Uposatha.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
To whatever extent the boundary marks have been proclaimed all around:
the Saṅgha appoints these boundary marks as the boundary for the Uposatha assembly.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of these boundary marks as the boundary for the Uposatha assembly, let him be silent; [if he does not approve, let him speak].
"Whoever does not approve may speak.
The Uposatha assembly has been authorized by the Saṅgha with these landmarks as its boundary.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I shall hold it to be so."
Now at that time, in a certain monastery on the Uposatha day, some junior monks, having assembled first,
departed [thinking], "The elders have not yet arrived."
The Uposatha was held at an improper time.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, on that very Uposatha day for the elder monks to assemble first.”
Now at that time, in Rājagaha, there were several monasteries within the same boundary.
There, the monks disputed, saying, "Let the Uposatha be performed in our monastery; let the Uposatha be performed in our monastery."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“In this case, monks, there are several residences that share the same boundary.
Therein, the monks fall into dispute:”
‘Let the Uposatha be performed in our residence; let the Uposatha be performed in our residence.
In that case, monks, all those monks must assemble together in one place and perform the Uposatha.
Or else, wherever an elder monk resides, they should assemble there and perform the Uposatha.
"But the Uposatha should not be performed by a Saṅgha that is incomplete.
Whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
7. The Authorization of the Non-separation Boundary (Avippavāsa-sīmā).
Now at that time, as the Venerable Mahākassapa was coming from Andhakavinda to Rājagaha for the Uposatha ceremony, he was swept away while crossing a river on the way, and his robes were wet.
The bhikkhus said to the Venerable Mahākassapa,
"Friend, why are your robes wet?"
“Here, friends, while coming from Andhakavinda to Rājagaha for the Uposatha, I was carried away by a river as I was crossing it on the way;
because of that, my robes became wet.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, whatever boundary has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence with a single Uposatha, let the Saṅgha authorize that boundary as ‘not being separated from the three robes.
And thus, monks, it should be authorized:
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:”
‘Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs.

That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence with a single Uposatha—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize that boundary as one where one is not separated from one’s three robes.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence for a single Uposatha, the Saṅgha now authorizes as a non-separation from the three robes.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the authorization of this boundary as a non-separation from the three robes, let him be silent."
"Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
This boundary has been authorized by the Saṅgha as one where one is not separated from the three robes.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this."
Now at that time, thinking that the Blessed One had authorized the permission not to be separated from the three robes, the monks deposited their robes within inhabited areas.
Those robes were lost, burnt, or gnawed by rats;
consequently, the monks became poorly clothed and wore coarse robes.
The bhikkhus said this:
“Friends, why are you poorly clad and wearing coarse robes? [They replied:
“Friends, because the Blessed One has authorized us not to be separated from our three robes, we have deposited our robes within the village.”
“Those robes have been lost or burnt, or gnawed by rats; therefore we are poorly clothed and wear coarse robes.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

“Monks, let the Saṅgha authorize that boundary which has been designated as a common residence with a single Uposatha as being one where one is not separated from the three robes, except for the village and its precincts.”
And furthermore, monks, she should be appointed in this way:
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.”

That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence for a single Uposatha—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize that boundary as one where one is not separated from the three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.

That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence for a single Uposatha, the Saṅgha now authorizes as a zone where one is not separated from one’s three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts.

Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the authorization of this boundary as a zone where one is not separated from one’s three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts, let him remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“That boundary has been approved by the Saṅgha as one where one is not separated from the three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
8. The Abolishing of the Boundary.
“Monks, when one is establishing a boundary, first the boundary for common affiliation must be established; afterwards, the non-separation from the three robes must be established.
Monks, when one is abolishing a boundary, first the non-separation from the three robes must be abolished; afterwards, the boundary for common affiliation must be abolished.
And this, monks, is how the non-separation from the three robes is to be abolished.”
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
That non-separation from the three robes which was authorized by the Saṅgha—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha rescind that authorization for non-separation from the three robes."
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs:
that which was authorized by the Saṅgha as non-separation from the three robes, the Saṅgha now revokes that non-separation from the three robes.
Whichever venerable one approves of the abolition of this non-separation from the three robes, let him be silent;
whichever does not approve, let him speak.
This non-separation from the three robes has been abolished by the Saṅgha.
‘The Saṅgha consents; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
And furthermore, monks, the boundary should be abolished in this way:
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: [He should speak as follows:]...’
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.

That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence with a single Uposatha—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha abolish that boundary as a common residence with a single Uposatha.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a single common residence with a single Uposatha—let the Saṅgha abolish that boundary as a single common residence with a single Uposatha.
Whichever venerable one approves of the abolition of this boundary as a single common residence with a single Uposatha, let him be silent."
"Whoever does not approve may speak.
This boundary has been abolished by the Saṅgha; it is a common residence with a single Uposatha.
It is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this."
9. Village Boundaries, etc.

“Monks, when a boundary has not been formally authorized and established, whatever village or town one dwells near, the village boundary of that village or the town boundary of that town constitutes there a common community and a single Uposatha.
Monks, in a forest that is devoid of villages, an area extending seven abbhantaras in every direction constitutes there a common community with a single Uposatha.
Monks, all rivers are not boundaries;
the entire ocean is not a boundary.
“Every lake is without boundary.

Whatever area, monks, extends from the center of a river, the ocean, or a lake to the distance of a splash of water on all sides for a man of medium height—this is the common residence there, with a single Uposatha.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were overlapping one boundary with another boundary.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, for those whose boundary was first authorized, that legal act is legitimate, irreversible, and fit to stand.
For those whose boundary was authorized later, bhikkhus, that legal act is illegitimate, reversible, and unfit to stand.”
“Monks, one boundary must not be made to overlap with another boundary.
Whoever should so overlap it commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were making one boundary encompass another boundary.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, for those whose boundary was first authorized, that legal act is legitimate, irreversible, and fit to stand.
For those whose boundary was authorized later, bhikkhus, that legal act is illegitimate, reversible, and unfit to stand.”
“Monks, one boundary must not encompass another boundary.
Whoever should so encompass it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you, when establishing a boundary, to establish the boundary after setting aside a space between boundaries.”
10. On the Breaking of the Uposatha, etc.
Then it occurred to the bhikkhus:
“How many kinds of Uposatha are there?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, there are these two Uposatha days: the fourteenth-day and the fifteenth-day. These, monks, are the two Uposatha days.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“How many kinds of Uposatha ceremonies are there?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of Uposatha ceremonies:”
An Uposatha procedure that is illegal and incomplete;
an Uposatha procedure that is illegal but complete;
an Uposatha procedure that is legal but incomplete.
"A Uposatha ceremony that is conducted according to the Dhamma and with a complete assembly.
In this regard, monks, as for that which is an Uposatha ceremony conducted contrary to the Dhamma and with an incomplete assembly: such a Uposatha ceremony, monks, should not be performed.
Nor was such a Uposatha ceremony authorized by me.
In this regard, monks, as for that which is a Uposatha procedure performed by a complete assembly in a manner contrary to the Dhamma:
such a Uposatha procedure, monks, should not be carried out;

nor was such a Uposatha procedure authorized by me. In this regard, monks, as for that which is a Uposatha procedure performed by a factional assembly in accordance with the Dhamma: such a Uposatha procedure, monks, should not be carried out.
Nor have I authorized such a Uposatha ceremony as that.

In this regard, monks, whatever Uposatha ceremony is performed according to the Dhamma by a unanimous assembly—that kind of Uposatha ceremony, monks, is to be performed; it is that kind of Uposatha ceremony which has been authorized by me.
Therefore, monks, we shall perform such a Uposatha ceremony as this: namely, one according to the Dhamma and with a unanimous assembly.
"For thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Then it occurred to the monks: "The recitation of the Pātimokkha, etc., has been given in brief."
“How many, indeed, are the recitations of the Pātimokkha?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha.”
Having recited the Nidāna, the remainder should be announced by means of hearing.
This is the first recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Having recited the Nidāna and having recited the four Pārājikas, the remainder should be announced by means of hearing.
This is the second recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Having recited the Introduction, having recited the four Pārājikas, and having recited the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, the remainder is to be announced by way of summary.
This is the third recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Having recited the Nidāna, having recited the four Pārājikas, having recited the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, and having recited the two Aniyatas, the remainder is to be announced by way of summary.
This is the fourth method of reciting the Pātimokkha.
The fifth is by way of full detail alone.
“Monks, these are the five ways of reciting the Pātimokkha.
Now at that time, the monks,
thinking, “The Blessed One has authorized a brief recitation of the Pātimokkha,” [proceeded accordingly].
They recited the Pātimokkha in brief at all times.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in brief."
“Whoever should recite it [in full], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, in a certain monastery in the Kosala country, on the Uposatha day, there was a threat from Savaras.
The bhikkhus were unable to recite the Pātimokkha in detail.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, when there is an obstacle, to recite the Pātimokkha in brief.
Now at that time, the group of six monks recited the Pātimokkha in brief even when there was no obstacle.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, when there is no obstacle, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in brief.
Whoever should recite it [in brief], there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
“I allow you, monks, when there is an obstacle, to recite the Pātimokkha in brief.

In this regard, these are the obstacles: a royal obstacle, a thief obstacle, a fire obstacle, a water obstacle, a human obstacle, a non-human obstacle, a beast obstacle, a creeping-creature obstacle, an obstacle to life, and an obstacle to the holy life.”
“I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha in brief when such obstacles exist, but in full detail when no obstacles exist.
Now at that time, the group of six monks spoke on the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha without being requested to do so.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, the Dhamma should not be spoken in the midst of the Saṅgha by one who has not been requested.
Whoever should speak it commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow an elder monk to either speak the Dhamma himself or to request another to do so.”
12. The Discussion on Asking about the Vinaya.
Now at that time, the group of six monks were asking about the Vinaya in the midst of the Saṅgha without being authorized.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, the Vinaya must not be questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha by one who has not been appointed.
Whoever should question it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to question the Vinaya in the midst of the Saṅgha by one who has been appointed.”
And furthermore, monks, it should be authorized in this way:
either one should authorize oneself, or another should authorize another.
And how should one authorize oneself?
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
If it is timely for the Saṅgha, I would ask such-and-such a question regarding the Vinaya."
In this way, one should be authorized by oneself.
And how should another be authorized by another?
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let such-and-such a person ask such-and-such a person about the Vinaya.
In this way, one person is to be authorized by another.”
Now at that time, well-behaved monks, having been authorized in the midst of the Saṅgha, were asking about the Vinaya.
The group-of-six monks became resentful, they became dissatisfied, and they threatened them with violence.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, even when authorized in the midst of the Saṅgha, to question someone regarding the Vinaya after surveying the assembly and weighing the individual.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, being unauthorized in the midst of the Saṅgha, answered questions on the Vinaya.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, the Vinaya must not be answered in the midst of the Saṅgha by one who has not been appointed.
Whoever should answer it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
"I allow you, monks, for one authorized in the midst of the Saṅgha to answer questions on the Vinaya.
And furthermore, monks, it should be authorized in this way:
either one may authorize oneself, or another may authorize another."
And how should one approve oneself?
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
‘If it is timely for the Saṅgha, being asked about the Vinaya by such-and-such a person, I would answer.
In this way one should appoint oneself.
And how is another to be appointed by another?
A competent and learned bhikkhu should inform the Saṅgha thus:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let such-and-such a person answer when questioned on the Vinaya by such-and-such a person.”
“In this way, one person should be formally authorized by another.
Now at that time, well-behaved monks, having been authorized in the midst of the Saṅgha, were answering questions on the Vinaya.
The group-of-six monks became resentful, they became dissatisfied, and they threatened them with death.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you, even when appointed in the midst of the Saṅgha, to answer a question on the Vinaya after surveying the assembly and weighing the individual.
14. Discussion on Rebuke.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were accusing a monk of an offense without having first granted him leave.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, a monk must not be accused of an offense without having been granted leave.”
Whoever should reprove [a monk] commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, I allow you to reprove someone for an offense only after having obtained his consent, saying:
"Venerable sir, please give me your consent; I wish to speak with you."
Now at that time, the well-behaved monks, having obtained leave from the monks of the group of six, were charging them with an offense.
The monks of the group of six became resentful, harbored ill will, and threatened them with violence.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, even when permission has been granted, to reprove someone for an offense after having weighed the individual.

Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, thinking, “The well-behaved monks are having us grant permission,” preemptively had pure monks who were without offenses grant them permission where there was no basis and no cause.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, an opportunity should not be requested from pure monks who are free of offenses, without basis and without cause.
Whoever should so request it commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, to grant an opportunity after having weighed the individual.”
15. Refutation of Illegal Acts, etc.
Now at that time, the group of six monks were performing illegal acts in the midst of the Saṅgha.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, an illegitimate legal procedure must not be carried out.
Whoever should carry one out commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Yet they continued to carry out an illegitimate legal procedure.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to protest when an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*) is being carried out.
Now at that time, the well-behaved monks protested when an illegitimate legal procedure was being carried out by the group of six monks.
The group of six monks harbored resentment, felt dissatisfaction, and threatened them with death.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [The Blessed One said:
“Monks, I allow you to disclose even one’s own view.”
They manifested their views in the very presence of those [monks].
The group-of-six monks felt resentment and dissatisfaction, and they threatened them with death.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to protest with four or five [monks], to reveal one’s view with two or three, and to resolve it with one, saying:
‘This is not acceptable to me.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, while reciting the Pātimokkha in the midst of the Saṅgha, intentionally did not let it be heard.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, the reciter of the Pātimokkha must not intentionally fail to announce [the offenses].
Whoever should fail to announce them commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī was the reciter of the Pātimokkha for the Saṅgha, and he had a cawing voice like a crow.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Udāyī:
"It has been laid down by the Blessed One—"
‘The reciter of the Pātimokkha must announce [the time]. But I have a voice like a crow; how, indeed, should I proceed?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow the reciter of the Pātimokkha to make an effort.”
‘How might I recite it?
There is no offense for one who makes such an effort.
At that time, however, Devadatta was reciting the Pātimokkha before an assembly that included laypeople.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly that includes householders.
Whoever should recite it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the group of six monks recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of the Saṅgha without being requested to do so.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, the Pātimokkha must not be recited in the midst of the Saṅgha by one who has not been requested.”
Whoever should recite it [in this manner], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
"I allow you, monks, the Pātimokkha with the elders at its head.
The first section on other sectarians is finished.
16. The Request for the Recitation of the Pātimokkha, etc.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagaha as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Codanāvatthu.
Wandering by stages on his tour, he arrived at Codanāvatthu.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were living in a certain residence.
There, a senior bhikkhu was ignorant and incompetent;
he did not know the Uposatha, nor the Uposatha ritual, nor the Pātimokkha, nor the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Then it occurred to those monks:
"The Blessed One has prescribed:

'The Pātimokkha is headed by the senior monk. Yet this senior monk of ours is ignorant and incompetent; he does not know the Uposatha, nor the Uposatha ritual, nor the Pātimokkha, nor the recitation of the Pātimokkha."
"How indeed should we proceed?
they asked, and reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"I allow you, monks, that whichever monk there is who is competent and capable, he should undertake the Pātimokkha on their behalf."
Now at that time, in a certain residence, on the Uposatha day, several monks were staying who were foolish and incompetent.
They did not know the Uposatha, nor the Uposatha ritual, nor the Pātimokkha, nor the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
They requested the Elder:
“Venerable sir, let the Elder recite the Pātimokkha.
He replied,
“Friend, it is not possible for me to do so.”
They requested the second elder:
"Venerable sir, let the elder recite the Pātimokkha.
He also spoke thus:
“It is not possible for me, friends,” he replied.
They then requested the third elder:
“Venerable sir, may the elder recite the Pātimokkha.”
He too said,
"Friend, it is not possible for me.
By this very means, they requested [the task] down to the most junior member of the Saṅgha.
“Venerable sir, please recite the Pātimokkha.
He replied,
“It is not possible for me to do so, venerable sir.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“In this case, monks, in a certain residence on that very Uposatha day, several monks are staying who are foolish and incompetent.
They do not know the Uposatha, nor the Uposatha ritual, nor the Pātimokkha, nor the recitation of the Pātimokkha.”
They request that elder:
"Venerable sir, may the elder recite the Pātimokkha.
He speaks thus:
‘Friend, it is not my turn.
They then request the second elder:
‘Venerable sir, may the elder recite the Pātimokkha.’
He too says,
“Friends, it is not possible for me.
They then request a third elder:
‘Venerable sir, let the Elder recite the Pātimokkha.
He too says thus:
‘It is not possible for me, friend.’
In this same manner, they request even the most junior member of the Saṅgha,
saying, “Venerable sir, please recite the Pātimokkha.
He too speaks thus:
‘Venerable sir, it is not possible for me.
In that case, monks, those monks should immediately dispatch one monk from a neighboring residence, saying:
‘Go, friend; having mastered the Pātimokkha either in brief or in detail, please return.’”
Then it occurred to the monks:
"By whom should he be sent away?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a senior monk to direct a junior monk.
When directed by the senior monk, the junior monks did not go.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who has been commanded by a senior monk must not fail to go if he is not ill.
Whoever does not go commits an offense of wrong-doing.
17. The Permission to Learn the Counting of Fortnights, etc.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Codanāvatthu for as long as he pleased, returned once more to Rājagaha.
Now at that time, people asked the bhikkhus who were walking for alms:
"Venerable sirs, what day of the fortnight is it?"
The bhikkhus said,
"We do not know, friend.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“These ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, do not even know how to count the fortnights; what else good could they possibly know?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to learn the counting of the fortnights.”
Then it occurred to the bhikkhus,
"By whom should the counting of the fortnight be learned?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, for all of you to learn the counting of the number of those present.
Now at that time, people asked the monks as they were walking for alms:
“Venerable sirs, how many monks are there?”
The bhikkhus said,
“We do not know, friend.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“These ascetics, the sons of the Sakyan, do not even know one another; how then will they know anything else that is wholesome?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to count the monks.”
Then it occurred to the monks,
"When indeed should the monks be counted?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, on that very day of the Uposatha, either to count by name or to distribute voting tickets.
Now at that time, monks who did not know that it was the Uposatha day went for alms as far as a distant village.
They arrived even while the Pātimokkha was being recited, and they arrived when the recitation had just finished.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“I allow you, monks, to announce: ‘Today is the Uposatha.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“By whom, then, should it be announced?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, the senior monk to announce the time.”
Now at that time, a certain elder did not remember the time.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to announce it even at the time of the meal,” [the Blessed One said].
Even at the time of the meal, they did not remember it.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to announce [the time] at whatever time one remembers it.”
18. Permission for Preliminary Duties.
Now at that time, in a certain residence, the Uposatha hall was dirty.
The visiting monks complained, grumbled, and were indignant, saying:
“How can it be that the resident monks do not sweep the Uposatha hall?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to sweep the Uposatha hall.”
Then it occurred to the bhikkhus:
“By whom, now, should the Uposatha hall be swept?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, for a senior monk to direct a junior monk.
When directed by the senior monk, the junior monks did not sweep.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who has been appointed by an elder and is not ill must sweep.
Whoever does not sweep commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, no seat had been prepared in the Uposatha hall.
The bhikkhus sat on the bare ground, and their limbs as well as their robes became covered in dust.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to prepare seats in the Uposatha hall,” he said.
Then it occurred to the monks:
"By whom, now, should the seats be prepared in the Uposatha hall?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, for a senior monk to direct a junior monk.
When directed by the senior monk, the junior monks did not set out [the seats].
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, when commanded by a senior monk, one who is not ill must provide illumination.
Whoever does not provide it commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, there was no lamp in the Uposatha hall.
In the darkness, the monks stepped on both their bodies and their robes.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to provide a lamp in the Uposatha hall.”
Then it occurred to the monks,
"By whom should a lamp be provided in the Uposatha hall?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a senior monk to direct a junior monk.
Although directed by the senior monk, the junior monks did not light the lamps.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who has been commanded by a senior monk and is not ill must light a lamp.
Whoever does not light it commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, in a certain residence, the resident monks neither set out drinking water nor set out water for washing.
The visiting monks complained, grumbled, and were indignant,
saying, "How can it be that the resident monks neither provide drinking water nor provide water for washing?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to provide drinking water and water for washing.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“By whom, now, should the drinking water and water for washing be provided?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a senior monk to command a junior monk.
